models.description:
# Model Summary

Four-model ensemble of ByT5-base fine-tuned for Akkadian-to-English machine translation, achieving **40.18 private LB** (9th / 2,673 teams, gold medal) in the [Deep Past Initiative](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/deep-past-initiative-machine-translation) Kaggle competition.

The ensemble translates 4,000-year-old Old Assyrian cuneiform transliterations into English. It uses source-grounded Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding with 13 faithfulness features to select the best translation from candidates generated by diverse models trained on different data compositions.

**Base architecture:** [google/byt5-base](https://huggingface.co/google/byt5-base) (582M parameters) — a byte-level sequence-to-sequence Transformer that tokenises at the byte level, avoiding vocabulary issues with Akkadian diacritics (š ṣ ṭ ḫ).

## Usage

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM

# Load one of the 4 checkpoints
model_path = "path/to/v12_gap_e3"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("google/byt5-base")
model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained(model_path)

# Translate
source = "Translate Akkadian to English: um-ma A-šùr-i-dí-ma a-na A-šùr-na-da qí-bi-ma"
inputs = tokenizer(source, return_tensors="pt", max_length=2048, truncation=True)
outputs = model.generate(
    **inputs,
    num_beams=12,
    num_return_sequences=4,  # Must be ≥2 on Kaggle (beam search bug)
    max_new_tokens=256,
    length_penalty=1.05,
)
translations = tokenizer.batch_decode(outputs, skip_special_tokens=True)
print(translations[0])
# "From Aššur-idī to Aššur-nādā"
```

The full ensemble pipeline (4-model SG-MBR scoring) is implemented in the [submission notebook](https://www.kaggle.com/code/eleftheria14/3-model-source-grounded-mbr-chrf-35-10-55).

**Known limitation:** `num_return_sequences=1` with `num_beams>1` silently produces garbled output on Kaggle's version of HuggingFace Transformers. Always use `num_return_sequences >= 2`.

## System

This is an ensemble of 4 models with a source-grounded MBR scoring layer:

1. **Input:** Akkadian transliteration with `{d}` curly determinatives, Unicode subscripts, `<gap>` markers. Test data uses `h` (not `ḫ`) — convert `h`→`ḫ` before inference.
2. **Generation:** Each model produces 4 beam search candidates (12 beams, top 4 returned).
3. **Selection:** Source-grounded MBR scores all 16 candidates (4 models × 4 each) using 13 features: gap count match, number preservation, Sumerogram translation correctness, divine name match, determinative semantics, repetition detection, length ratio, name coverage, name spelling, echo detection, Sumerogram residue, content grounding, document type match.
4. **Post-processing:** Gap normalisation, fraction conversion (ḫ→h, decimals→Unicode), annotation removal (fem./sing./pl.), name repair via fuzzy matching against the OA onomasticon.
5. **Output:** English translation.

## Implementation requirements

**Training:**
- Hardware: NVIDIA DGX Spark GB10 (128GB unified memory) and NVIDIA H100 (80GB)
- Precision: FP32 (critical — BF16 costs 12+ LB points on ByT5)
- Optimiser: Adafactor with label smoothing 0.2
- Training time: ~4 hours per model on H100, ~8 hours on GB10
- Total compute: ~4 models × ~6 hours average = ~30 GPU-hours

**Inference:**
- Runs on Kaggle T4 (16GB) within the 9-hour notebook time limit
- 4 models loaded sequentially (not simultaneously) — each ~2.2GB in FP16
- Beam search: 12 beams, 4 candidates per model
- Wall time: ~3 hours for 4,000 test samples on T4

# Model Characteristics

## Model initialisation

All 4 models are **fine-tuned** from [google/byt5-base](https://huggingface.co/google/byt5-base), a pre-trained byte-level T5 model. No additional pre-training (DAPT was tried but hurt performance — see solution writeup).

## Model stats

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Base model | google/byt5-base |
| Parameters | 582M per model |
| Precision | FP32 (training), FP16 (inference) |
| Encoder layers | 12 |
| Decoder layers | 4 |
| d_model | 1,536 |
| d_ff | 3,968 |
| Vocab size | 384 (byte-level + special tokens) |
| Max input length | 2,048 bytes |
| Max output length | 256 bytes |
| Checkpoint size | ~2.2 GB per model (safetensors) |
| Total ensemble size | ~9.3 GB (4 models) |

## Ensemble composition

| Model | Checkpoint | What's different | Training data | LR | Selection |
|-------|------------|-----------------|---------------|-----|-----------|
| **A — Soup** | v11_soup | Real data only, weight-averaged 3 checkpoints | ~125K real pairs | 1e-4 | Soup of epochs 3/5/6 (40/30/30%) |
| **B — Gap** | v12_gap_e3 | 2-stage: base → gap fine-tune | ~166K real + ~124K gap pairs | 1e-4 | Gap epoch 3 |
| **C — Joint** | v14_gap_e3 | Higher LR, encoder freeze, expanded data | ~127K real + ~124K gap pairs | 3e-4 | Gap epoch 3 |
| **D — Distribution** | v16_e6 | Distribution-matched 80/20 real/augmented blend | ~130K real + 40K augmented | 1e-4 | Epoch 6 |

All models: google/byt5-base, FP32, Adafactor, label smoothing 0.2, bidirectional training (Akkadian→English + English→Akkadian), competition data 3× upsampled, dynamic batching (8192 token budget).

## Other details

The model is not pruned, quantized, or distilled. FP16 is used at inference only (as a lightweight regulariser — observed +0.1 LB improvement over FP32 inference). No differential privacy techniques were applied.

# Data Overview

## Training data

~189K unique real translation pairs + ~101K synthetic/augmented pairs extracted from 12 sources. Full dataset available at [akkadian-english-translation-pairs](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/eleftheria14/akkadian-english-translation-pairs).

| Source | Pairs | Period |
|--------|-------|--------|
| PDF extraction (publications.csv) | 94,893 | Mixed (mostly OA) |
| AKT volumes (13 editions) | 15,534 | Old Assyrian |
| Akkademia RINAP | 33,226 | Neo-Assyrian |
| OARE sentence pairs | 6,823 | Old Assyrian |
| Competition train | 1,561 + 4,315 | Old Assyrian |
| GOA grammar (Kouwenberg) | 2,210 | Old Assyrian |
| Others (Larsen, secondary, Prague, eSAD) | ~3,800 | Mixed |
| Vision re-extraction | 30,793 | Mixed |
| Entity-swap augmented | 39,062 | Old Assyrian |
| Composed + synthetic | 61,630 | Old Assyrian |

Data was cleaned through 30+ iterative OCR repair passes validated against 91 automated invariants. See [DATA_PROVENANCE.md](https://github.com/Eleftheria14/Deep-Past-Solution/blob/main/docs/DATA_PROVENANCE.md) for full citations.

## Demographic groups

Not applicable. The training data consists of ancient Akkadian cuneiform texts (~2000–1700 BCE) and their English scholarly translations. No demographic attributes are present.

## Evaluation data

- **Training split:** 90/10 random hold-out (seed 42)
- **Eval metric:** chrF (character n-gram F-score) per epoch
- **Final evaluation:** Competition leaderboard (geometric mean of BLEU and chrF++)
- **Notable difference:** Internal eval chrF consistently diverged from LB score — checkpoint selection was ultimately LB-driven

# Evaluation Results

## Summary

| Setup | Public LB | Private LB |
|-------|-----------|------------|
| Single model (soup of 3 checkpoints) | 37.7 | 37.6 |
| Single model + gap training | 38.9 | 37.3 |
| Multi-checkpoint MBR (1 model) | 39.6 | 38.4 |
| **4-model SG-MBR ensemble** | **39.2** | **40.18** |

Cross-model diversity with source-grounded MBR gained +0.98 on private LB (39.2→40.18), while multi-checkpoint MBR of one model inflated on public and dropped −1.2 on private.

## Subgroup evaluation results

No formal subgroup analysis was performed. Informal observations:
- **Gap-heavy sources** (>50% tokens are `<gap>`): Lower translation quality — model tends to output generic filler.
- **Neo-Assyrian sources** (Akkademia data): Lower accuracy than Old Assyrian, as the model is primarily trained on OA.
- **Name-heavy texts** (witness lists, seal inscriptions): Higher error rate due to novel name hallucination.

## Fairness

Not applicable — this is a historical text translation model, not a model making decisions about people.

## Usage limitations

- **Domain:** Trained primarily on Old Assyrian commercial texts (~2000–1700 BCE). Performance on other Akkadian dialects (Neo-Assyrian, Old Babylonian, Standard Babylonian) is lower.
- **Gap handling:** The model handles `<gap>` markers in source but may hallucinate content for heavily damaged texts.
- **Named entities:** Personal names (PN) and geographic names (GN) are the largest source of errors. The post-processing pipeline includes fuzzy name repair, but novel names not in the training lexicon may be mistranslated.
- **FP32 required:** Training must use FP32. BF16 causes severe quality degradation (12+ LB points loss) due to byte-level precision requirements.

## Ethics

This model translates ancient scholarly texts and poses minimal direct ethical risk. The training data is derived from published academic editions of cuneiform tablets, with appropriate citations. The model may produce inaccurate translations — outputs should be verified by qualified Assyriologists before use in academic publications.

# Cognitive Load Balance

Trained on the [Are Your Employees Burning Out?](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/blurredmachine/are-your-employees-burning-out) dataset (HackerEarth ML Challenge, ~18.5k samples). The model classifies burnout risk into Low / Medium / High based on 6 workplace features.

The most interesting result: **Mental Fatigue Score alone explains 61.6%** of the prediction. Resource Allocation (workload) adds another 26%. Everything else — gender, company type, remote work — is basically noise (<1% each). Burnout is a load problem, not a context problem.

Two variants:
- **base** — DecisionTree, depth=5, 87.7% acc, 7 KB. You can actually inspect the decision paths.
- **large** — RandomForest, 100 trees, 88.9% acc, 2.8 MB. Better at catching High-risk cases (precision 0.91 vs 0.79).

I binned the continuous Burn Rate (0–1) into three classes: Low (<0.33), Medium (0.33–0.66), High (>0.66). The dataset is imbalanced — 58% Medium, 28% Low, 14% High — which is why High-risk recall matters.

### Features

1. Mental Fatigue Score (0–10, self-reported) — 61.6%
2. Resource Allocation (1–10, workload) — 26.3%
3. Designation (0–5, seniority) — 10.6%
4. WFH Setup Available — <1%
5. Gender — <1%
6. Company Type — <1%

### Usage

The pickle contains a dict, not a raw model:

```python
import pickle

with open('model.pkl', 'rb') as f:
    b = pickle.load(f)

b['model'].predict([[1, 0, 1, 4.0, 8.0, 7.0]])  # → ['High']
# b['features']      — column order
# b['feature_meta']  — encoding maps (Female=0, Male=1, etc.)
# b['labels']        — ['Low', 'Medium', 'High']
# b['metrics']       — test_accuracy, cv_mean, cv_std
```

### What this doesn't capture

Six features is obviously not enough for real burnout prediction. Sleep, relationships, autonomy, meaning — none of that is in the data. The fatigue score is self-reported and subjective. There's no temporal dimension (fatigue accumulation over days/weeks). And it's trained on one dataset, never validated elsewhere.

Still, the signal is clear: if you track just two numbers — fatigue and workload — you get a surprisingly useful risk estimate.

Apache 2.0. Training data: ODC-By.

instances.overview: DecisionTree, depth=5. 87.7% test accuracy (5-fold CV: 87.8% ± 0.5%). Tiny at 7 KB — you can inspect every split.

Also in the bundle: `features` (column names), `feature_meta` (encoding maps), `labels`, `metrics` (accuracy, CV scores), `training_samples` (14872), `test_samples` (3718).

Use this variant when you need interpretability or minimal footprint. Use **large** when catching High-risk cases matters more (precision 0.91 vs 0.79 here).
